newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul gold market quiet for holiday, sees revival.
newsitem.headline: Seoul gold market quiet for holiday, sees revival.

text.p: The South Korean gold market was quiet this week with most local retailers closed for the Lunar New Year holiday, dealers in Seoul said on Tuesday.
But the domestic market was expected to pick-up from Wednesday as the dampening effects on sentiment from the financial crisis at the Hanbo steel group begin to fade.
Domestic retailers will open up shop on Wednesday after being closed from January 6.
"We expect the gold market to revive tomorrow after the long Lunar New Year holiday," a dealer with Tong Yang Global said.

He said domestic gold demand should also be bolstered by improved industrial offttake, particularly in the dental and bonding wire sectors, following the sharp retreat in bullion prices on the international market.

Gold producer LG Metals' daily selling price for the precious metal, which is regarded as a benchmark for the local bullion wholesale market, fell by 50 won per gram to 10,000 won on Tuesday from 10,050 won a week ago.
But LG's silver price rose by two won a gram to 154 won, in line with more stable world silver prices, compared with 152 won a week earlier.
Traders said the ripples from the Hanbo scandal were now being felt more acutely in political circles and were lessening in the business sector.
"We can't see any impact from the Hanbo debacle this week on the domestic gold market," the Tong Yang dealer said.
On Monday, South Korean prosecutors summoned two rulling party members of parliament to determine if they accepted kickbacks from Hanbo and pressured bankers into offering loans to the company.

The two are the first politicians to be investigated over loans totalling five trillion won ($5.8 billion) provided to Hanbo Steel, flagship of the Hanbo Group and South Korea's second largest steelmaker, before it became insolvent in late January.
South Korean domestic gold prices fell in line with weak international prices, but the decline was partially offset by the won's sharp decline against the dollar, dealers said.
The won has tumbled in line with the Japanese yen's weakness against the dollar on world markets and on South Korea's rising trade deficit.
South Korea posted a record monthly trade deficit of $3.48 billion for January, compared with $2.13 billion a year earlier.
The telegraphic transfer selling rate for customers, posted by the Korea Exchange Bank, rose to 871.20 won against the dollar from 870.20 a week ago.
The rate is regarded as a benchmark for local foreign exchange rates by South Korean companies.
